Journey · Children’s Books

“We should develop wholesomeness. Nobody likes to (p. 31–45)

Pages 31–45 (15 pages)
Page 31

“We should develop wholesomeness. Nobody likes to hear unpleasant words. We can change our habits little by little. When someone is complaining he is thinking of himself first, whereas when he thinks of the other person’s feelings he forgets about himself.” Energy. Right effort, viriya (energy), is another perfection. Alan spoke about the effort it takes to come on a journey like this one: “In many ways the Dhamma is not easy for me. I have to take long trips on my own to see Acharn. My family and friends are not interested at all, so one has to go against the stream. It takes quite an effort to turn away from what most people follow and to go your own way. It is important to accumulate19 right effort; without it one could not develop right understanding at all.” Effort made for the Dhamma is never wasted: “It can condition us to make an effort in the future to listen to the Dhamma again.” Renunciation. Nekkhamma (renunciation) means giving up. “Not only monks20 but also laypeople21 can develop this perfection. Right understanding of nāma and rūpa can condition renunciation.” Giving up here does not mean leaving home. It means seeing what appears as it is: “There can be understanding of visible object22 as just visible object, not the dear person we love.” Acharn Sujin said to Nina: “It is very difficult to realize that visible object is just visible object, not Lodewijk”. Visākhā. Nina tells of a woman at the Buddha’s time who lived in the world and still practised letting go: “At the age of seven she became a sotāpanna, after she heard the Buddha preach. Later on she married and she had ten sons and ten daughters. She had perfect generosity and she was always attending to the needs of the Sangha. She was called the laydisciple who was foremost23 in ministering24 to the Sangha. She was attached25 to her husband, children and grandchildren, but she was aware of all that naturally arose in her daily life. She understood her clinging26 as a conditioned27 reality28, not self.” A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 31

Page 32

“She was called the laydisciple who was foremost in ministering to the Sangha.” A sotāpanna (stream-enterer) is a person who has reached the first stage of enlightenment. The Saṅgha (the order) is the community of monks. Visākhā’s example “teaches us not to ignore attachment when it arises, but to be aware of it. It is natural to have attachment, but paññā (wisdom) can understand it, no matter how strong it is.” Acharn Sujin said about lobha (attachment): “It is just a reality, don’t worry about it. Follow it with understanding. You can see how it changes. It is most important to understand it as not self. Whatever arises is conditioned.” Truthfulness. Visākhā also had sacca (truthfulness). “Truthfulness means not deluding29 oneself about the realities which naturally arise, including defilements.” A person who believes that he can stop himself from clinging is not being truthful. ““That is only make belief, not truthfulness”, Acharn said.” The ascetic who told the truth. Nina ends with a story from the Harita Jātaka (the birth story of Harita), number 431. The Bodhisatta lived as an ascetic30 in the royal park, and the King gave him food every day. Once, when the King had to go away because of trouble at the frontier, the ascetic’s old defilements rose up “like a poisonous snake lying in a box”, and he broke his good conduct. When the King came back, he asked the ascetic whether the bad rumours31 about him were true. The ascetic thought: “If I say that I did not indulge32 in sin, the King would believe me, but in this world there is no surer foundation than truthful speech. Someone who forsakes the truth cannot attain Buddhahood, even if he sits in the sacred enclosure of the Bodhi Tree. Hence I should only speak the truth.” A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 32

Page 33

“Thus, he spoke the truth to the King.” “Thus, he spoke the truth to the King.” He went back to the forest, regained jhāna (deep calm of mind), and at the end of his life was reborn33 in the plane34 of the Brahmās (highest heavenly beings35). Nina writes: “We should be truthful, we should see our clinging which has been accumulated for aeons and not ignore it.” And she takes courage from the story: “Although we have accumulated many kinds of defilements for aeons, right understanding of whatever appears can be developed so that eventually enlightenment can be attained.” HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. wholesome: good and healthy for the mind: giving, kindness, patience, understanding 2. perfection: a good quality made as full and strong as it can be 3. generosity: giving freely and gladly 4. morality: good conduct; not killing, not stealing, not lying and the rest 5. renunciation: giving up; letting go of what one is attached to 6. energy: effort; the strength that keeps on going 7. truthfulness: always telling the truth and keeping to it 8. determination: making up one's mind firmly and keeping to it 9. loving-kindness: wishing others well; friendliness to everyone 10. equanimity: an even, calm mind that is not shaken by good luck or bad 11. enlightenment: the moment when the truth is seen fully and for good, and the dirt of the mind is cut away 12. condition: something that has to be there before another thing can happen 13. arise: to come up; to begin; to happen 14. defilement: something that makes the mind dirty: wanting, anger, not knowing and the rest 15. innumerable: too many to count 16. eradicate: to root out completely, so that it can never come back 17. aeon: a huge stretch of time, far longer than anyone can count 18. abstain: to hold back from doing something, such as lying 19. accumulate: to gather up bit by bit, so that there is more and more of it 20. monk: a man who has left home to follow the Buddha's rule of life A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 33

Page 34

21. lay: an ordinary person who follows the teaching while living at home 22. object: the thing that a moment of mind knows: a colour, a sound, a thought 23. foremost: first; the best 24. ministering: serving and looking after 25. attachment: wanting something and holding on to it; liking that will not let go 26. clinging: holding on tightly; not wanting to let go 27. conditioned: made to happen by other things; it could not come up on its own 28. reality: something that is really there, not only a name or an idea 29. delusion: being fooled; not seeing things as they are 30. ascetic: a person who gives up home and comfort to live simply and seek the truth; or that hard way of living 31. rumour: a story passed from person to person that may not be true 32. indulge: to give in to something one enjoys, too much 33. rebirth: being born again in a new life after this one ends 34. plane: a world or level where beings live: the human world, the heavens, the animal world and so on 35. being: any living creature: a person, an animal, a heavenly being A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 34

Quiz 3 (chapters 5 and 6) The answers are at the back. 1. After seeing the golden treasures, what does saññā (remembrance) do? (a) it falls away at once and leaves nothing (b) it remembers what is seen, and cittas think of it for a long time (c) it makes the treasures disappear (d) it sees the treasures again 2. Acharn Sujin asked: “Where is that being?” What did she say a being is? 3. When Nina said that one has to be prepared for the death of someone dear, what did Acharn Sujin say? (a) There is plenty of time. (b) Now you are preparing. (c) Do not think about it. (d) Nobody can prepare. 4. True or false: Acharn Sujin said that one must try to prevent thinking. 5. In the simile of the actors on the stage, what are the bhavaṅga-cittas (life-continuum consciousness)? (a) the actors (b) the darkness in between the acts, when the curtain is drawn (c) the audience (d) the stage itself 6. What is praise called, and why is it dangerous? 7. Name the ten perfections as Nina lists them. 8. What did Acharn Sujin say her goal with mettā (loving-kindness) was? (a) infinite mettā (b) to extend mettā to different people at any time, and not to particular people (c) mettā only for her friends (d) mettā only on special days 9. Chapter 7: Nobody with sati What is in the way? Nina’s third chapter opens with a question: “What hinders1 the development of satipaṭṭhāna?” Her answer is short. “The idea of self is in the way.” People want sati (awareness2), and the wanting itself is the trouble: “instead of attending to what appears at the present moment we continue to think of a concept3 of sati “we” wish to have.” “Why do you want it?” Alan asked Acharn Sujin: “Why does understanding not arise4 often?” She answered: “Why do you want it? Develop it.” Nina calls this “a short but pointed reminder; it helped us to know our clinging5 to understanding.” Then she writes: “We want to be “somebody with sati”, but it is more beneficial6 to remember that we are “nobody”. That is in accordance with the truth. There is no self who could plan to have sati.” Not planning. Acharn Sujin said: “The right Path is not planning when and where sati will arise. We should not have any idea of “I will develop right understanding”.” Nina said that clear understanding is not possible until vipassanā ñāṇa (insight7 knowledge) has arisen, a stage at which realities8 are seen directly as they are. Acharn turned her back to the present: “We do not have to think of insight knowledge, what about understanding of this moment? If we can understand this moment as it is with awareness, then understanding will continue to develop.” Then came a very short exchange. Acharn: “Are you wishing for that stage?” Nina: “Yes.” Acharn: “If you don’t wish but you develop it, it is more beneficial.” Nina: “But I cannot help wishing for it.” Acharn: “If you understand that wishing is of no use, there is a condition9 for awareness.” Acharn added: “When insight knowledge arises it is not Nina who has attained it; there is at that very moment nobody.” The Buddha taught paramattha dhammas (ultimate10 realities) “so that one can understand the meaning of no being, no person, no self. It is citta which knows an object11, not a person.” Seeing is conditioned now. Alan put it in his own way: “Seeing is conditioned12 now, we do not have to try to see. Hearing is conditioned now, we do not have to try to hear. Vipassanā ñāṇa, insight knowledge, is anattā, it is beyond control.” Anattā (non-self13) means that nothing is anyone’s and nothing obeys anyone. Acharn agreed: “No matter how much you would like the arising of awareness, it cannot arise at will, by one’s wish. But whenever a moment of awareness arises, it is developing. That is why it takes aeons14. When we do not expect any result15, there will be result, because of the right cause.” Nina confessed: “When there is a short moment of considering realities, I cling to it, I spoil it again.” Acharn: “There are conditions for such moments. There is no you in reality.” And: “Only paññā can know when lobha arises.” “You can’t prevent it.” Another of Acharn Sujin’s remarks: “When there are conditions for awareness, you can’t prevent it from arising”. Nina explains: “When the conditions are right it must arise and we do not have to do anything to cause its arising.” Some people think they must first sit down and concentrate16 A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 37

Page 38

on their breathing in order to be calm. But true calm “is freedom from akusala”, and a person concentrating on breath may not notice when lobha (attachment17) is behind it. “The reality appearing at this moment has to be understood.” No fixed order. Some people read the Visuddhimagga (the Path of Purity18) and think it lays down a rule: first sīla (morality19), then samādhi (concentration), then paññā (understanding). Nina writes that Buddhaghosa, its author, was describing the different levels of each, not a timetable: “There is no rule with regard to a specific order of the development of the different types of kusala.” Jhāna (deep calm of mind) is not needed first. Its aim is calm, “not the understanding of nāma and rūpa as dukkha, impermanent20 and anattā”. Never lost. “All the moments of studying and considering the Dhamma and all the other kinds of kusala are never lost, they are accumulated21 from one moment to the next moment so that they can arise again, later on.” The opposite is also true. Acharn Sujin “helped us to see that moments of akusala are wasted moments of our life, that they delay the development of paññā.” Be considerate first. A person who wants sati (awareness) and forgets the other kinds of kusala (wholesome22) is still thinking of himself. Acharn Sujin said: “Instead of wanting to develop satipaṭṭhāna, one should develop kusala, being considerate23 for others.” Nina writes: “Kindness, considerateness, patience, all wholesome cetasikas are conditions for the arising of different levels of sati and pañña.” Then she describes three levels of paññā (understanding): “One level of paññā is seeing the disadvantage24 of akusala, another level of paññā is studying and considering the Dhamma, and another level again is paññā developed in satipaṭṭhāna.” level 1 seeing the disadvantage of akusala noticing that impatience is useless, that aversion is ugly level 2 studying and considering the Dhamma reading, listening, discussing, thinking it over level 3 paññā developed in satipaṭṭhāna directly knowing seeing as seeing, sound as sound, not self all three are paññā (understanding); kindness, considerateness and patience are conditions for all of them “One level of paññā is seeing the disadvantage of akusala, another level of paññā is studying and considering the Dhamma, and another level again is paññā developed in satipaṭṭhāna.” Do not give up. Some people give up because they think they cannot reach enlightenment25 in this life. That too is the self in the way: “they have an idea of “I want to try”.” Acharn Sujin’s answer was always the same: ““Develop it now, be aware now”, Acharn often said.” And: ““Just begin again and again, so that there is more understanding of realities”, Acharn said.” Not like scholars. Acharn Sujin warned against learning the teaching the wrong way: A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 38

Page 39

“All realities are described in the texts, but how many times does sati arise? Develop it. The book is there, but the moment understanding develops is the most important. People learn Abhidhamma without knowing its real purpose, namely, the development of understanding of realities. They want to learn like scholars26.” The bud on the tree. Then she gave the travellers a picture to keep: “Paññā is like a bud which will appear on a tree. One does not know where and when it will appear. We should not care when it will appear; what about the understanding of this moment? If there is no understanding of this moment, develop it now.” “Paññā is like a bud which will appear on a tree.” Nina writes: “It is like the bud on a tree, when it is the right time nobody can stop it from appearing and then it will bloom.” When insight knowledge arises, “There is no self and no world at that moment.” But it passes “very quickly”, like a flash, and “Just a flash is not enough, all daily realities have to be fully understood.” After it, “the world full of people appears again”, and the work goes on. HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. hinder: to get in the way of; to hold back 2. awareness: noticing what is really there right now; another word for mindfulness 3. concept: an idea put together by thinking, such as 'tree' or 'person'; it cannot be seen or touched by itself 4. arise: to come up; to begin; to happen 5. clinging: holding on tightly; not wanting to let go 6. beneficial: helpful; good for someone 7. insight: seeing into something; here, seeing clearly for oneself that there is only mind and matter 8. reality: something that is really there, not only a name or an idea 9. condition: something that has to be there before another thing can happen 10. ultimate: the deepest and most real; what is really there when all the names are taken away A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 39

11. object: the thing that a moment of mind knows: a colour, a sound, a thought 12. conditioned: made to happen by other things; it could not come up on its own 13. non-self: not a self; not a person; not anyone's 14. aeon: a huge stretch of time, far longer than anyone can count 15. result: what comes later from a deed done before, as fruit comes from a seed 16. concentration: keeping the mind on one thing 17. attachment: wanting something and holding on to it; liking that will not let go 18. purify: to make clean; cleanness 19. morality: good conduct; not killing, not stealing, not lying and the rest 20. impermanent: not lasting; passing away 21. accumulate: to gather up bit by bit, so that there is more and more of it 22. wholesome: good and healthy for the mind: giving, kindness, patience, understanding 23. considerate: thinking of other people's feelings 24. disadvantage: the harm or trouble that comes with something 25. enlightenment: the moment when the truth is seen fully and for good, and the dirt of the mind is cut away 26. scholar: a learned person who studies books A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 40

Chapter 8: Colours, sounds and the stream Two worlds. Nina writes: “When we are not aware of ultimate1 realities2, we live in the conventional3 world. When visible object4 appears we think immediately of “something” or “someone”, we are thinking of concepts5. Thinking of concepts conceals the characteristic6 of visible object.” People think they see cars, houses and friends. “We usually think of people and things, but seeing sees only different colours.” Acharn Sujin put it in a way the travellers kept: “When we look at somebody it is exactly the same as looking at a painting, Acharn said.” “When we look at somebody it is exactly the same as looking at a painting, Acharn said.” Colours. Alan began a talk about what seeing really sees: “When we see, we can think of many colours, like red, green or yellow. That is thinking. Visible object is not many colours, it is only one colour.” Acharn asked him what visible object meant. “It is seen through the eyesense.” She went on: “Do we have to name it red, green or yellow? The reality which appears is not yet understood as a mere dhamma.” Then she corrected the idea of one colour: “Not only one colour appears, there are conditions7 for different colours to appear. Nobody can change the conditions for each different colour. You cannot change the colour of Gabi’s eyes. Colour is just a kind of rūpa which can be seen through the eyes. We do not have to name colour blue, black or green. It is the same in the case of sound, there are many different sounds. Nobody can change the conditions for each different sound. Sound is just a reality and it is not self who experiences8 it. There is nobody. If awareness9 does not arise10 it is always ‘I’ who hears.” Cars and houses. Nina said: “We look at cars and houses all the time, it seems that we see them.” Acharn: “It can be realized that visible object is different from the thought of a car.” Nina: “Seeing sees details, but it does not know the meaning of them.” Acharn: “It sees everything that is visible. When we are reading, A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 41

Page 42

we are thinking, but there is also the seeing of visible object.” The marks on the page are seen; the words and their meaning are thought. Nina said: “If these would not appear through the eyes, we could not read.” visible object colour: rūpa (matter) it knows nothing seeing through the eye-door sees only what is visible then thinking: “a car” through the mind-door a concept, put together by memory “When we are reading, we are thinking, but there is also the seeing of visible object.” two different realities, at two different moments “It can be realized that visible object is different from the thought of a car.” Acharn Sujin then said what the whole journey was for: “We will understand our task in life: the development of understanding of realities. Even when there is a little more understanding of realities it means that we are on the right way.” A noisy room. Nina slept in a noisy hotel room and heard people walking past and talking. “However, it helps to remember that hearing is only vipāka, that it is impossible to control it.” Hearing is vipāka (result11), the result of past kamma (deed12). Nobody chooses it. Acharn Sujin said: “We can realize that it is only a moment that is conditioned13. All dhammas in a day appear as just dhammas when there is awareness and right understanding.” “I always follow the stream.” In Istanbul a show had been planned, and Nina worried that it would end very late. Acharn Sujin “said that she would not worry once she happened to be there. She said: “I always follow the stream”.” Nina still remembers it when she is at a party and cannot leave when she wants to. “When we try to change events we are bound to have aversion14 and we have no patience. When we “follow the stream” we can understand that all events are only conditioned dhammas.” The frontier city. Nina ends her chapter with verse 315 of the Dhammapada (the Buddha’s verses on the teaching): “Even as a frontier city is well guarded both within and without, Evenso one should guard oneself; let not a moment slip. For they who let the moments slip, mourn, delivered over to Hell.” A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 42

Page 43

“Evenso one should guard oneself; let not a moment slip.” A frontier city stands at the edge of a kingdom. Its walls are guarded day and night, inside and out. Nina applies the verse to moments of the mind: “When we do not act, speak or think with kusala cittas, there are akusala cittas and we let the moments of our life slip. We should “guard ourselves”, but without any idea of “self”.” The guard is sati (awareness), not a person. Her last words on this part of the journey: “There are opportunities for the development of right understanding in any situation and this conditions more patience. Our journey with Dhamma was most beneficial15.” HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. ultimate: the deepest and most real; what is really there when all the names are taken away 2. reality: something that is really there, not only a name or an idea 3. conventional: the ordinary everyday way of talking, as when a pile of parts is called a chariot 4. object: the thing that a moment of mind knows: a colour, a sound, a thought 5. concept: an idea put together by thinking, such as 'tree' or 'person'; it cannot be seen or touched by itself 6. characteristic: the mark by which something is known; what is special about it 7. condition: something that has to be there before another thing can happen 8. experience: to know, see, hear or feel something; or the knowing itself 9. awareness: noticing what is really there right now; another word for mindfulness 10. arise: to come up; to begin; to happen 11. result: what comes later from a deed done before, as fruit comes from a seed 12. deed: something done; an act, good or bad 13. conditioned: made to happen by other things; it could not come up on its own 14. aversion: not liking something and wanting it to go away; anger, even a little 15. beneficial: helpful; good for someone A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 43

Quiz 4 (chapters 7 and 8) The answers are at the back. 1. Alan asked: “Why does understanding not arise often?” What did Acharn Sujin answer? (a) Because you do not try hard enough. (b) Why do you want it? Develop it. (c) It will come in time. (d) Read more books. 2. True or false: Nina writes that it is more beneficial to be “somebody with sati” than to be “nobody”. 3. Acharn asked Nina: “Are you wishing for that stage?” Nina said yes. What did Acharn say was more beneficial? 4. Complete Acharn Sujin’s words: “It is citta which knows an object, not …” (a) a person. (b) a cetasika. (c) a rūpa. (d) a book. 5. What did Acharn Sujin say happens when there are conditions for awareness? (a) one must sit down first (b) you can’t prevent it from arising (c) it will arise tomorrow (d) it must be planned 6. True or false: the Visuddhimagga (the Path of Purity) lays down a rule that sīla (morality) must be developed first, then samādhi (concentration), then paññā (understanding). 7. Name the three levels of paññā (understanding) that Nina describes. 8. Acharn Sujin said that paññā (understanding) is like … (a) a river (b) a bud which will appear on a tree (c) a lamp (d) a suitcase 9. Acharn Sujin said that looking at somebody is exactly the same as … (a) looking in a mirror (b) looking at a painting (c) reading a book (d) hearing a sound 10. What did Acharn Sujin say about the colour of Gabi’s eyes, and what was her point? 11. In Istanbul, when Nina worried that a show would end very late, what did Acharn Sujin say? (a) We will leave early. (b) I always follow the stream (c) Shows are a waste of time. A Journey with Dhamma for Young Readers · 44
